extracted.intended_audience: scientific authors preparing responses to peer reviewers (manuscript authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting a clear, complete, and professional 'response to reviewers' document to accompany a revised manuscript submitted to a peer-reviewed journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1: Provide an overview, then quote the full set of reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the response letter with a summary of changes (pointing out new data and analyses done in response to the most essential criticisms), then include the complete set of reviews with your responses interleaved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may include figures and tables for reviewers' benefit that are not intended for the manuscript/supplement; mention these in your introduction. If a criticism is raised by multiple reviewers, point that out in the summary. The overview should highlight the most important changes before the detailed, interleaved responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 2: Be polite and respectful of all reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a polite, respectful tone in all responses, even if you believe the reviewer is uninformed, biased, or discourteous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume misunderstandings may reflect unclear manuscript text; consider revising rather than insulting. If you suspect reviewer misconduct or conflict (vengeance/competitor), do not confront the reviewer publicly—communicate concerns separately to the editor. Rudeness from a reviewer does not justify rudeness from you; keep the goal of publishing in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 3: Accept the blame
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reviewer failed to understand something, apologize for not making it clear and consider revising the text (even if you believe it was already clear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, quote the revised text in your response. Even seemingly unnecessary requested changes are often better implemented to show the reviewer they were heard and understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 4: Make the response self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote changes to text or figures directly in the response so reviewers don't have to flip back and forth between the manuscript and the response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible indicate specific line numbers and state whether they refer to the original or revised manuscript. Exception: very long new text (e.g., a whole new section) can be alluded to explicitly (give the new section title) rather than quoted in full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 5: Respond to every point raised by the reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Address every critique in the review; do not ignore points even if you disagree with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit when a single bullet contains multiple issues — respond to each separately. It's acceptable to interleave responses and to break up a single bullet with multiple responses; this is usually clearer than combining multiple replies into one block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 6: Use typography to help the reviewer navigate your response
rubrics_metrics.description: Use typeface changes, color, and indenting to distinguish between the review text, your responses, and the changes made to the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the typographical conventions in the introduction to your response so reviewers know which text corresponds to reviews, answers, and manuscript edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 7: Whenever possible, begin your response to each comment with a direct answer to the point being raised
rubrics_metrics.description: Start each reply with a concise, direct answer (a 'yes' or 'no' when possible), then provide background or supporting discussion afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it immediately clear whether you agree with the reviewer; if the reviewer is correct, state so. Use the brief direct answer to show you took the comment seriously before elaborating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8: When possible, do what the reviewer asks
rubrics_metrics.description: Comply with reviewers' reasonable requests for additional analyses, experiments, or changes when possible; if you perform the requested work, report the results in your response and explain whether they belong in the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you think a requested analysis is uninformative or flawed, do it anyway, report the results, and explain why it should or should not be included. Consider acknowledging reviewers for substantial contributions when appropriate (but note some journals disallow reviewer acknowledgments). If requests exceed the scope of your work, explain that tactfully — but be cautious about dismissing many requests as 'outside scope' or you may fail to satisfy the reviewer. For conflicts between reviewer and editor requests (e.g., shorten vs. add detail), seek editor discretion. Examples: moving content between supplement and main text should be done with editor agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 9: Be clear about what changed relative to the previous version
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state whether the cited text or changes were present in the previous version or are new in the revised manuscript, and describe the exact changes made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wording that merely points to text in the manuscript without clarifying whether it is newly added. Reference explicitly both previous and revised versions (and line numbers if used) so reviewers can tell what is new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10: If necessary, write the response twice
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider drafting an initial, candid 'venting' response to process critiques and then writing a separate, polished response document to send to reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the first draft to analyze options and vent frustrations; wait and then create a second formal document after doing some work to address critiques. This helps transform emotional reactions into professional, constructive replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate letter to the managing editor when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a separate letter to the editor to raise concerns about reviewer behavior, potential conflicts of interest, or conflicting reviewer requests and journal policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this private letter to describe possible reviewer conflicts, vengeful behavior, or to request editor discretion when reviewer requests conflict with each other or with journal policy. This keeps sensitive issues out of the public response document while ensuring editors are informed.
